Daniel — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Daniel came from a noble family, perhaps even Judah's royal family.

According to the historical chronology given in Henry's introduction, Daniel was taken captive to Babylon in the fourth year of Jehoiachin, in 606 BC, while still young.

He was educated in the learning of the Chaldeans and held high office under both the Babylonian and Persian empires.

He suffered persecution for his faith but was miraculously delivered.

Henry estimates that Daniel was about ninety-four years old at the time of his last visions.

The book is partly historical, describing events affecting Daniel and the Jewish people in Babylon.

It is, however, chiefly prophetic.

Its visions and prophecies concern the four great world empires, the coming and death of the Messiah, the restoration of the Jews and the conversion of the Gentiles.

Some prophetic passages are very difficult to explain.

Nevertheless, throughout the book we find encouragement to faith and hope, examples to follow and teaching that directs our thoughts to Jesus Christ on the cross and upon his glorious throne.

Daniel and his companions are taken to Babylon (verses 1–7)

In the first year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, captured Jerusalem and carried away the people and possessions he chose.

Henry notes that most interpreters date the seventy years of captivity from this first deportation.

It is in a ruler's interest to employ wise people.

A wise ruler will identify and educate people with such abilities. Nebuchadnezzar therefore ordered the chosen young men to receive instruction.

The Hebrew names of these youths each contained a reference to God.

Their pagan captors gave them new names associated with idolatry, intending to make them forget the God of their ancestors, who had guided them since their youth.

It is painful to consider how frequently public education corrupts people's principles and moral conduct.

The young men refuse the king's food (verses 8–16)

Whatever influence or favor we gain with others must be recognized as God's gift.

Daniel remained steadfast in his religion.

Whatever name others gave him, he retained the spirit of an Israelite.

The young men were concerned that eating the king's food might involve sin.

When God's people live in Babylon, they must take particular care not to share in its sins.

Young people deserve praise when they refuse to chase sensual pleasures.

Anyone hoping to grow in wisdom and godliness should learn early to practice self-control.

Daniel was determined not to defile himself by sin.

We should fear sin far more than any outward suffering.

It is easier to keep temptation at a distance than to resist it once it is near.

When other people favor us, we can make no better use of that favor than to ask their help in keeping us from sin.

People often fail to believe that avoiding excess and eating moderately can benefit bodily health until they try.

Conscientious self-restraint will bring more comfort even in the present life than sinful indulgence.

The young men grow in wisdom (verses 17–21)

Daniel and his companions remained true to their religion.

God rewarded them with outstanding knowledge and learning.

Godly young people should try to become more capable in useful work than their peers.

Their aim should not be human applause but the honor of the gospel and preparation to serve others effectively.

A country benefits—and its ruler receives honor—when those in authority can identify the people best suited for particular responsibilities and promote them accordingly.

Young people should seriously consider this chapter.

Everyone should remember that God honors those who honor him, while people who despise him will be treated lightly.

[Dan.1.1-Dan.1.7]
Daniel
Daniel was of noble birth, if not one of the royal family of Judah. He was carried captive to Babylon in the fourth year of Jehoiachin, B. C. 606, when a youth. He was there taught the learning of the Chaldeans, and held high offices, both under the Babylonian and Persian empires. He was persecuted for his religion, but was miraculously delivered; and lived to a great age, as he must have been about ninety-four years old at the time of the last of his visions. The book of Daniel is partly historical, relating various circumstances which befel himself and the Jews, at Babylon; but is chiefly prophetical, detailing visions and prophecies which foretell numerous important events relative to the four great empires of the world, the coming and death of the Messiah, the restoration of the Jews, and the conversion of the Gentiles. Though there are considerable difficulties in explaining the prophetical meaning of some passages in this book, we always find encouragement to faith and hope, examples worthy of imitation, and something to direct our thoughts to Christ Jesus upon the cross and on his glorious throne.
Chapter 1
The captivity of Daniel and his companions. ( [Dan.1.1-Dan.1.7] Dn 1:1-7) Their refusal to eat the king's meat. ( [Dan.1.8-Dan.1.16] Dn 1:8-16) Their improvement in wisdom. ( [Dan.1.17-Dan.1.21] Dn 1:17-21)
Verses 1-7 Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, in the first year of his reign, took Jerusalem, and carried whom and what he pleased away. From this first captivity, most think the seventy years are to be dated. It is the interest of princes to employ wise men; and it is their wisdom to find out and train up such. Nebuchadnezzar ordered that these chosen youths should be taught. All their Hebrew names had something of God in them; but to make them forget the God of their fathers, the Guide of their youth, the heathen gave them names that savoured of idolatry. It is painful to reflect how often public education tends to corrupt the principles and morals.
[Dan.1.8-Dan.1.16]
Verses 8-16 The interest we think we make for ourselves, we must acknowledge to be God's gift. Daniel was still firm to his religion. Whatever they called him, he still held fast the spirit of an Israelite. These youths scrupled concerning the meat, lest it should be sinful. When God's people are in Babylon they need take special care that they partake not of her sins. It is much to the praise of young people, not to covet or seek the delights of sense. Those who would excel in wisdom and piety, must learn betimes to keep the body under. Daniel avoided defiling himself with sin; and we should more fear that than any outward trouble. It is easier to keep temptation at a distance, than to resist it when near. And we cannot better improve our interest in any with whom we have found favour, than to use it to keep us from sin. People will not believe the benefit of avoiding excess, and of a spare diet, nor how much they contribute to the health of the body, unless they try. Conscientious temperance will always do more, even for the comfort of this life, than sinful indulgence.
[Dan.1.17-Dan.1.21]
Verses 17-21 Daniel and his fellows kept to their religion; and God rewarded them with eminence in learning. Pious young persons should endeavour to do better than their fellows in useful things; not for the praise of man, but for the honour of the gospel, and that they may be qualified for usefulness. And it is well for a country, and for the honour of a prince, when he is able to judge who are best fitted to serve him, and prefers them on that account. Let young men steadily attend to this chapter; and let all remember that God will honour those who honour him, but those who despise him shall be lightly esteemed.

Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by his dream (verses 1–13)

The greatest rulers are often especially troubled by worries and anxieties.

These may keep them awake at night, while ordinary laborers sleep deeply and peacefully.

We seldom know the uneasiness experienced by people who live amid great splendor and what others imagine to be pleasure.

The king demanded that his learned men reveal the dream itself.

If they failed, he would have them executed as deceivers.

People are often more eager to know future events than to discover the way of salvation or the path of duty.

Yet knowledge of the future often increases anxiety and distress.

The king condemned people who had deceived him by claiming to possess extraordinary powers, but now demanded that they do something beyond what they had professed to be able to do.

Daniel and his companions pray for an answer (verses 14–23)

Daniel humbly prayed that God would reveal the king's dream and its meaning.

Friends who pray for us are valuable friends.

Even the greatest and best people should welcome the prayers of others.

We ought to show that we appreciate such friends and their prayers.

Daniel and his companions prayed specifically.

Whatever we request, we can expect to receive it only as a gift of God's mercy.

He invites us to bring our needs, burdens and dangers before him.

They appealed to God because of the grave danger they faced.

The mercy they sought was granted.

The earnest prayers of righteous people accomplish much.

Daniel thanked God for revealing what would save his and his companions' lives.

How much more grateful should we be that God reveals the salvation of our souls, even to people who are not counted among the world's wise and educated!

Daniel speaks before the king (verses 24–30)

Daniel corrected the king's opinion of magicians and diviners.

The inability of created beings should direct us toward the all-sufficient Creator.

God can do for us and disclose to us what no one on earth can, especially the work of redemption and the secret purposes of his love within it.

Daniel confirmed that the dream was important because it concerned the kingdoms and changing affairs of this world.

Those whom God has greatly honored should put away every thought of their own wisdom or merit, so that the Lord alone receives praise for the good they possess and accomplish.

The image and the kingdoms (verses 31–45)

The image represented successive earthly empires that would dominate nations and affect the affairs of the Jewish church.

Henry interprets its parts as follows.

First, the head of gold: the Chaldean Empire, then in power.

Second, the chest and arms of silver: the empire of the Medes and Persians.

Third, the belly and thighs of bronze: the Greek Empire, founded by Alexander.

Fourth, the legs and feet of iron: the Roman Empire.

Henry further understands the ten toes as ten kingdoms into which Rome would divide.

Some would be weak like clay, others strong like iron.

Attempts to reunite them into a stronger empire would prove unsuccessful.

These are Henry's interpretations of the vision, not independently established details supplied in its symbols.

The stone cut without human hands represents the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Christ's kingdom would rise amid earthly kingdoms and overthrow Satan's kingdom within them.

He is the stone the builders rejected, precisely because human hands had not shaped him.

He has nevertheless become the chief cornerstone.

Christ's government and peace will increase without end.

The Lord will reign not only until time ends, but after time itself is no more.

Henry believes the events fulfilled so far correspond closely to the vision, while future ages will see the stone break the whole image and fill the earth.

Daniel and his companions are honored (verses 46–49)

Our duty is to direct everyone's attention toward the Lord, the Author and Giver of all good gifts.

Some people recognize God's power and majesty without choosing to serve him themselves.

But everyone should seek God's glory and the greatest good of humankind.

Nebuchadnezzar's golden image (verses 1–7)

Henry supposes that the image's height—about thirty yards—probably included a pedestal.

He also considers it likely that the image was covered with gold plates, not cast from a solid mass of gold.

Pride and religious intolerance lead rulers to require everyone to follow their religion, whether it is true or false.

When worldly advantage attracts and harsh punishment frightens, few people resist.

Those who are careless, devoted to bodily pleasures or without faith find it especially easy to follow the crowd.

Almost any evil can be made attractive through music and celebration, or enforced through the threat of fire.

False worship has often been established and maintained through such methods.

The three men refuse to worship (verses 8–18)

True devotion tends to make a person calm, gentle and peaceful.

Superstition and devotion to false gods, by contrast, can inflame passion.

The king's demand was simple: bow down or burn.

Proud people still challenge God's authority, asking why they should fear him.

Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego did not hesitate about their duty.

They did not allow concern for life or death to override it.

When an invitation or threat plainly asks us to commit sin, we must not bargain with the temptation.

We should reject it at once, as Christ said, “Get behind me, Satan.”

The men gave a direct answer rather than inventing an evasive one.

Those who put obedience first can entrust the consequences to God.

The Lord can control and overrule all the powers arrayed against his people.

Lord, if you will, you can deliver us.

If God is for us, we need not fear human opposition.

He may deliver us from death or through death.

We must obey God rather than people, suffer rather than sin, and never do wrong in the hope of producing something good.

God's preserving them from sinful compromise was as remarkable a miracle in the sphere of grace as his preserving them from the furnace was in the natural world.

Fear of people, love of the world and especially lack of faith cause surrender to temptation.

Strong confidence in the truth helps us avoid denying Christ or being ashamed of him.

Our answers should be gentle but firm.

God preserves them in the furnace (verses 19–27)

Nebuchadnezzar could heat the furnace as much as he wished.

Its fire could torment those cast into it only for a short time.

Henry contrasts that earthly fire with the unending torment of final judgment, referring to Revelation 14:10–11.

The event fulfilled the promise of Isaiah 43:2: those passing through the fire would not be consumed.

The three men left it to the God who preserved them within the fire to bring them out.

They walked in the midst of the flames, sustained and encouraged by the presence of the Son of God, as Henry identifies their companion.

Those who suffer for Christ likewise have his presence amid suffering, whether in a fiery furnace or in the valley of the shadow of death.

Nebuchadnezzar acknowledged them as servants of the Most High God, who could save them from his power.

God himself is the consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29).

If we could see into the eternal world, we would see persecuted believers safe from their enemies while the impenitent persecutors faced God's judgment.

Nebuchadnezzar praises God (verses 28–30)

This miracle helped the Jewish captives remain faithful to their religion and reject idolatry.

It deeply impressed Nebuchadnezzar with God's power.

But at this time it produced no lasting transformation of his conduct.

The God who preserved these faithful Jews in the furnace can also sustain us through temptation and keep us from falling into sin.

He who preserved these pious Jews in the fiery furnace, is able to uphold us in the hour of temptation, and to keep us from falling into sin.

Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges God's power (verses 1–18)

The beginning and end of this chapter encourage us to hope that Nebuchadnezzar became an example of the power of divine grace and the riches of mercy.

After recovering from his madness, he told people far away and left a written account for later generations of how God had justly humbled and graciously restored him.

When a sinner comes to his senses, he wishes to benefit others by telling them about God's wonderful mercy.

Before explaining the judgment brought upon him for pride, Nebuchadnezzar described the warning he had received in a dream.

The meaning was explained to him.

The person represented would lose his honor and the use of his reason for seven years.

This is surely among the most severe temporal judgments.

Whatever outward affliction God allows us to suffer, we should bear it patiently and be thankful if he preserves our reason and a peaceful conscience.

Even the dreadful loss of reason would be preferable to being allowed to multiply sins or disgrace God's name without restraint.

God as the righteous Judge had determined the matter, and heaven's angels approved it.

This does not mean that God requires the angels' counsel or agreement. The language expresses the solemnity of the sentence.

Henry also connects the demand with the word of the holy ones—God's afflicted people, whose cries the Lord hears.

Let us seek blessings that can never be taken away, and especially avoid pride and forgetting God.

Daniel explains the dream (verses 19–27)

Daniel was astonished and frightened by the severity of the announced judgment against such a powerful king.

He gave his counsel with tenderness and respect.

Genuine repentance requires not only ceasing to do evil but also learning to do good.

Such repentance might not prevent every judgment.

Yet it might delay the trouble or shorten its duration.

Everyone who repents and turns to God will escape everlasting misery.

The king is humbled and restored (verses 28–37)

Pride and self-importance are particular temptations for powerful people.

They readily claim for themselves the glory that belongs only to God.

While the king's boast was still in his mouth, God's powerful word came.

Nebuchadnezzar lost his understanding and memory, and the powers of his rational mind failed.

We should beware of conduct that provokes God to remove our reason.

God opposes the proud.

The king wanted to be greater than a human being.

God justly brought him into a condition lower than a human being.

The Most High God lives forever.

His kingdom, like himself, is eternal and universal. No one can resist his power.

People can truly hope for divine honor only when they honor God, confess their sins and acknowledge his sovereign rule.

God not only restores what was lost through the sin of the first Adam, but adds glory through the righteousness and grace of the second Adam, Christ.

Afflictions last no longer than the period needed to accomplish the purpose for which God sent them.

Henry concludes that Nebuchadnezzar truly repented and became an accepted believer.

He also reports the view that Nebuchadnezzar lived no more than about a year after this restoration.

Thus the Lord knows how to humble those who walk in pride and give grace and comfort to the humble, brokenhearted sinner who calls upon him.

Verses 1-18 The beginning and end of this chapter lead us to hope, that Nebuchadnezzar was a monument of the power of Divine grace, and of the riches of Divine mercy. After he was recovered from his madness, he told to distant places, and wrote down for future ages, how God had justly humbled and graciously restored him. When a sinner comes to himself, he will promote the welfare of others, by making known the wondrous mercy of God. Nebuchadnezzar, before he related the Divine judgments upon him for his pride, told the warnings he had in a dream or vision. The meaning was explained to him. The person signified, was to be put down from honour, and to be deprived of the use of his reason seven years. This is surely the sorest of all temporal judgments. Whatever outward affliction God is pleased to lay upon us, we have cause to bear it patiently, and to be thankful that he continues the use of our reason, and the peace of our consciences. Yet if the Lord should see fit by such means to keep a sinner from multiplying crimes, or a believer from dishonouring his name, even the dreadful prevention would be far preferable to the evil conduct. God has determined it, as a righteous Judge, and the angels in heaven applaud. Not that the great God needs the counsel or concurrence of the angels, but it denotes the solemnity of this sentence. The demand is by the word of the holy ones, God's suffering people: when the oppressed cry to God, he will hear. Let us diligently seek blessings which can never be taken from us, and especially beware of pride and forgetfulness of God.
[Dan.4.19-Dan.4.27]
Verses 19-27 Daniel was struck with amazement and terror at so heavy a judgment coming upon so great a prince, and gives advice with tenderness and respect. It is necessary, in repentance, that we not only cease to do evil, but learn to do good. Though it might not wholly prevent the judgment, yet the trouble may be longer before it comes, or shorter when it does come. And everlasting misery will be escaped by all who repent and turn to God.
[Dan.4.28-Dan.4.37]
Verses 28-37 Pride and self-conceit are sins that beset great men. They are apt to take that glory to themselves which is due to God only. While the proud word was in the king's mouth, the powerful word came from God. His understanding and his memory were gone, and all the powers of the rational soul were broken. How careful we ought to be, not to do any thing which may provoke God to put us out of our senses! God resists the proud. Nebuchadnezzar would be more than a man, but God justly makes him less than a man. We may learn to believe concerning God, that the most high God lives for ever, and that his kingdom is like himself, everlasting, and universal. His power cannot be resisted. When men are brought to honour God, by confession of sin and acknowledging his sovereignty, then, and not till then, they may expect that God will honour them; not only restore them to the dignity they lost by the sin of the first Adam, but add excellent majesty to them, from the righteousness and grace of the Second Adam. Afflictions shall last no longer than till they have done the work for which they were sent. There can be no reasonable doubt that Nebuchadnezzar was a true penitent, and an accepted believer. It is thought that he did not live more than a year after his restoration. Thus the Lord knows how to abase those that walk in pride, but gives grace and consolation to the humble, broken-hearted sinner who calls upon Him.

Here is an earnest request to God to restore the poor captive Jews to their former enjoyments. O Lord, hearken and do. Not hearken and speak only, but hearken and do; do that for us which none else can do; and defer not. Here are several pleas and arguments to enforce the petitions. Do it for the Lord Christ's sake; Christ is the Lord of all. And for his sake God causes his face to shine upon sinners when they repent, and turn to him. In all our prayers this must be our plea, we must make mention of his righteousness, even of his only. The humble, fervent, believing earnestness of this prayer should ever be followed by us.
[Dan.9.20-Dan.9.27]
Verses 20-27 An answer was immediately sent to Daniel's prayer, and it is a very memorable one. We cannot now expect that God should send answers to our prayers by angels, but if we pray with fervency for that which God has promised, we may by faith take the promise as an immediate answer to the prayer; for He is faithful that has promised. Daniel had a far greater and more glorious redemption discovered to him, which God would work out for his church in the latter days. Those who would be acquainted with Christ and his grace, must be much in prayer. The evening offering was a type of the great sacrifice Christ was to offer in the evening of the world: in virtue of that sacrifice Daniel's prayer was accepted; and for the sake of that, this glorious discovery of redeeming love was made to him. We have, in verses 24-27, one of the most remarkable prophecies of Christ, of his coming and his salvation. It shows that the Jews are guilty of most obstinate unbelief, in expecting another Messiah, so long after the time expressly fixed for his coming. The seventy weeks mean a day for a year, or 490 years. About the end of this period a sacrifice would be offered, making full atonement for sin, and bringing in everlasting righteousness for the complete justification of every believer. Then the Jews, in the crucifixion of Jesus, would commit that crime by which the measure of their guilt would be filled up, and troubles would come upon their nation. All blessings bestowed on sinful man come through Christ's atoning sacrifice, who suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God. Here is our way of access to the throne of grace, and of our entrance to heaven. This seals the sum of prophecy, and confirms the covenant with many; and while we rejoice in the blessings of salvation, we should remember what they cost the Redeemer. How can those escape who neglect so great salvation!

Daniel sees a glorious figure by the Hiddekel (verses 1–9)

This chapter begins Daniel's final vision, which continues to the end of the book.

A long period would pass before all its events were fulfilled, and Henry says that much remained unfulfilled in his own day.

Henry identifies the glorious figure appearing to Daniel as Christ.

That appearance should lead us to think of him with great honor and reverence.

We should marvel that he humbled himself for our salvation.

Daniel lost all strength before the vision.

Even the greatest and most godly human beings cannot bear an unrestricted revelation of divine glory.

No one can see it and live.

But glorified believers will see Christ as he is and will be able to endure and enjoy that sight.

Even when Christ seems terrifying to people convicted of sin, his word contains enough comfort to calm their hearts.

The messenger explains future events (verses 10–21)

Whenever we draw near to God in fellowship, we should remember the immeasurable distance between sinful creatures and the holy Lord.

We are dust and ashes. How can we speak before the Lord of glory?

Nothing more effectively revives discouraged believers than the assurance that God loves them.

From the first day we turn toward him in duty, he is ready to meet us in mercy.

He is eager to hear prayer.

After describing coming events, the angel was to return and oppose measures by Persian kings that would harm the Jewish people.

Angels serve God as his messengers and helpers (Hebrews 1:14).

The rulers of Persia would do much evil against the Jews with God's permission.

Yet they would have done far greater harm if God had not prevented it.

The messenger would explain God's purposes more fully, though the prophecies give only their outline.

We should study what is written in the Scriptures of truth, because they concern our eternal peace.

Satan, his angels and evil advisers may incite rulers to harm the church.

We may rejoice that Christ our Prince and his powerful angels act against our enemies.

But we should not expect this hostile world to provide us with many supporters.

Nevertheless, all God's purposes will stand.

[Dan.10.1-Dan.10.9]
Chapter 10
Daniel's vision near the river Hiddekel. ( [Dan.10.1-Dan.10.9] Dn 10:1-9) He is to expect a discovery of future events. ( [Dan.10.10-Dan.10.21] Dn 10:10-21)
Verses 1-9 . This chapter relates the beginning of Daniel's last vision, which is continued to the end of the book. The time would be long before all would be accomplished; and much of it is not yet fulfilled. Christ appeared to Daniel in a glorious form, and it should engage us to think highly and honourably of him. Let us admire his condescension for us and our salvation. There remained no strength in Daniel. The greatest and best of men cannot bear the full discoveries of the Divine glory; for no man can see it, and live; but glorified saints see Christ as he is, and can bear the sight. How dreadful soever Christ may appear to those under convictions of sin, there is enough in his word to quiet their spirits.
[Dan.10.10-Dan.10.21]
Verses 10-21 Whenever we enter into communion with God, it becomes us to have a due sense of the infinite distance between us and the holy God. How shall we, that are dust and ashes, speak to the Lord of glory? Nothing is more likely, nothing more effectual to revive the drooping spirits of the saints, than to be assured of God's love to them. From the very first day we begin to look toward God in a way of duty, he is ready to meet us in the way of mercy. Thus ready is God to hear prayer. When the angel had told the prophet of the things to come, he was to return, and oppose the decrees of the Persian kings against the Jews. The angels are employed as God's ministering servants, Heb. 1:14. Though much was done against the Jews by the kings of Persia, God permitting it, much more mischief would have been done if God had not prevented it. He would now more fully show what were God's purposes, of which the prophecies form an outline; and we are concerned to study what is written in these Scriptures of truth, for they belong to our everlasting peace. While Satan and his angels, and evil counsellors, excite princes to mischief against the church, we may rejoice that Christ our Prince, and all his mighty angels, act against our enemies; but we ought not to expect many to favour us in this evil world. Yet the whole counsel of God shall be established; and let each one pray, Lord Jesus, be our righteousness now, and thou wilt be our everlasting confidence, through life, in death, at the day of judgment, and for evermore.
